paragraphs.title: The Promise of Redemption and the Gathering of Israel

answers: Because the Lord has redeemed him
Because Babylon protects him
Because he will never face trouble
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Fear not: for I have redeemed thee.”

answers: He will be with Israel
He will abandon Israel
He will stop the waters from existing
easy.explanation: The Lord promises, “I will be with thee.”
easy.q: What does the Lord promise when Israel passes through the waters?

answers: Only from the east
From the east, west, north, and south
Only from the north
easy.explanation: The Lord says He will bring Israel from the east and west and gather them from the north and south.
easy.q: From which directions will the Lord gather Israel?

answers: Because the Lord is with and protects Israel
Because Israel never enters water or fire
Because the waters and fire are powerless by themselves
medium.explanation: The Lord promises that the rivers will not overflow Israel and that the flame will not burn him.
medium.q: Why will the waters and fire not destroy Israel?

answers: The Lord values and loves Israel
The Lord has forgotten Israel
The Lord wants to destroy Israel
medium.explanation: The verse connects Israel’s preciousness, honor, and the Lord’s love.
medium.q: What does the statement that Israel was “precious” in the Lord’s sight show?

answers: A price given in exchange for someone
A place of worship
A military victory
medium.explanation: The Lord says He gave Egypt, Ethiopia, and Seba for Israel as a ransom.
medium.q: What does “ransom” mean in this passage?

answers: Israel was created for the Lord’s glory, so He gathers those called by His name
Israel was created to remain scattered
The passage gives no connection between creation and gathering
challenge.explanation: The Lord says He created and formed His people for His glory and then promises to gather them.
challenge.q: How are Israel’s creation and gathering connected?

answers: From protection and redemption to the gathering of sons and daughters
From gathering to permanent exile
From love to destruction
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from redemption and protection to the gathering of Israel from the ends of the earth.
challenge.q: What movement is described in these verses?

answers: That the people belong to the Lord
That the people have no connection with the Lord
That only foreign nations are included
challenge.explanation: The phrase identifies the gathered people as those belonging to the Lord and created for His glory.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by the phrase “every one that is called by my name”?

paragraphs.title: Israel as God’s Witness and God’s Uniqueness

answers: Israel and the servant whom He has chosen
The armies of Babylon
The nations alone
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Ye are my witnesses... and my servant whom I have chosen.”
easy.q: Who are called the Lord’s witnesses?

answers: That the Lord is the only God
That many gods are equal
That the Lord cannot save
easy.explanation: The passage teaches that no God was formed before the Lord or after Him.
easy.q: What were Israel to know and believe?

answers: The kings of the nations
The Lord alone
The witnesses of Israel
easy.explanation: The Lord declares, “beside me there is no saviour.”
easy.q: Who is the Savior according to these verses?

answers: So they may present witnesses and prove their claims
So they may gather Israel
So they may escape judgment
medium.explanation: The nations are challenged to declare, show former things, and bring forth witnesses.
medium.q: Why are all the nations gathered together?

answers: By knowing and believing that the Lord is God and Savior
By remaining silent
By worshipping the kings of the earth
medium.explanation: Israel witnesses through knowing, believing, and understanding who the Lord is.
medium.q: How does Israel serve as a witness?

answers: Another or foreign god
A faithful witness
A human ruler
medium.explanation: The Lord says there was no strange god among Israel, emphasizing His uniqueness.
medium.q: What does “strange god” mean in this context?

answers: Israel witnesses for the Lord, while the nations must prove their claims
The nations are the Lord’s witnesses, but Israel is not
There is no difference between them
challenge.explanation: Israel is called the Lord’s witness, while the nations are challenged to produce evidence.
challenge.q: What is the main difference between Israel and the nations in this passage?

answers: No one can prevent or undo what He does
Anyone can easily stop His work
The Lord does not act Himself
challenge.explanation: The statement presents the Lord’s work as unstoppable.
challenge.q: What does “I will work, and who shall let it?” teach about the Lord’s actions?

answers: They repeatedly state that there is no God or Savior beside Him
They describe Him as one of many saviors
They say another god existed before Him
challenge.explanation: The passage says there was no God before or after Him and no Savior beside Him.
challenge.q: How do the verses emphasize the Lord’s uniqueness?

paragraphs.title: The Fall of Babylon and the Way of Redemption

answers: For Israel’s sake
For Egypt’s sake
For Babylon’s sake
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “For your sake I have sent to Babylon.”
easy.q: For whose sake did the Lord send to Babylon?

answers: He brings down their nobles and subdues them
He makes them kings over Israel
He hides them in the wilderness
easy.explanation: The Lord says He has brought down Babylon’s nobles and the Chaldeans.
easy.q: What does the Lord do to Babylon and the Chaldeans?

answers: In the sea and in the mighty waters
In a palace
On a mountain only
easy.explanation: He is described as the One “which maketh a way in the sea, and a path in the mighty waters.”
easy.q: Where does the Lord make a way and a path?

answers: It opens the way for Israel’s redemption and return
It prevents Israel from returning
It cancels the promise of redemption
medium.explanation: The fall of Babylon removes the power holding the exiles and prepares the way for their return.
medium.q: How does Babylon’s fall relate to Israel’s return?

answers: The defeat of a mighty army
The strength of Babylon’s army
The return of the Chaldeans
medium.explanation: They lie down together and do not rise, showing that the army has been overcome.
medium.q: What does the fallen chariot, horse, army, and power picture?

answers: A way or road
A wall
A battle
medium.explanation: The word describes a route through the mighty waters.

answers: The powerful army is defeated and cannot rise against the Lord
The army is stronger than the Lord
The passage does not mention an army
challenge.explanation: Although the army has chariots, horses, and power, it is extinguished and unable to rise.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the army’s strength and the Lord’s power?

answers: It shows that the Lord can make a way where escape seems impossible
It shows that the sea prevents Israel’s return
It describes ordinary sea travel
challenge.explanation: A path through the sea symbolizes the Lord’s ability to open a way for His people.
challenge.q: Why does the way through the sea fit the theme of redemption?

answers: The Lord sends judgment against Babylon, defeats its army, and opens a way
Babylon grows stronger, defeats Israel, and closes every way
Israel is scattered, the sea is destroyed, and redemption ends
challenge.explanation: The verses connect Babylon’s defeat with the Lord’s power to make a way.
challenge.q: What sequence of ideas appears in the passage?

paragraphs.title: The New Deed in the Wilderness

answers: The former things and things of old
The sons and daughters
The rivers and waters
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old.”
easy.q: What does the Lord tell Israel not to remember or consider?

answers: A new thing
The same thing only
Nothing in the wilderness
easy.explanation: He declares, “Behold, I will do a new thing.”
easy.q: What is the Lord about to do?

answers: A way and rivers
Walls and armies
Cities and palaces
easy.explanation: He promises to make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.
easy.q: What does the Lord make in the wilderness?

answers: The way allows them to travel, and the waters give them drink
They prevent the people from moving
They are provided only for armies
medium.explanation: The new way supports travel, while the rivers give drink to the Lord’s people.
medium.q: How do the way and the waters help God’s people?

answers: The Lord’s people, His chosen
The army of Babylon
The kings of the nations
medium.explanation: The Lord gives water “to give drink to my people, my chosen.”
medium.q: For whom are the waters in the wilderness provided?

answers: A wild, desolate region
A crowded city
A stormy sea
medium.explanation: The wilderness is a deserted place through which the Lord makes a way and provides water.
medium.q: What does “wilderness” mean in this context?

answers: Because the Lord is directing attention to the new work He will do
Because the former miracles never happened
Because the Lord has no connection with the past
challenge.explanation: The command prepares Israel to recognize the new deed that is springing forth.
challenge.q: Why is Israel told not to focus on former things?

answers: They honor the Lord because He provides water in the wilderness
They stop the rivers from flowing
They attack the people
challenge.explanation: The beasts of the field honor the Lord because He gives water in the desert.
challenge.q: How are the animals connected with the new deed?

answers: That they might show forth the Lord’s praise
That they might hide His works
That they might conquer the wilderness
challenge.explanation: The Lord says, “This people have I formed for myself; they shall shew forth my praise.”
challenge.q: What is the purpose of forming this people?

paragraphs.title: Israel’s Sins and Its Failure to Serve God Properly

answers: Israel has not called upon Him
Israel has called upon Him too often
Israel has gathered the nations
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “But thou hast not called upon me, O Jacob.”
easy.q: What complaint does the Lord make at the beginning of this section?

answers: The small cattle of the burnt offerings
Water from the wilderness
A great army
easy.explanation: The Lord says Israel had not brought the small cattle of its burnt offerings.
easy.q: What had Israel not brought to the Lord?

answers: Israel’s sins and iniquities
The sacrifices themselves
The waters and fire
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “thou hast made me to serve with thy sins” and wearied Him with iniquities.

answers: Israel failed to honor the Lord properly but burdened Him with sins
Israel offered perfect worship and did not sin
Israel did absolutely nothing
medium.explanation: The passage contrasts neglected worship with the burden of Israel’s sins.
medium.q: What contrast appears between Israel’s worship and its sins?

answers: Because He says the sins and iniquities wearied Him
Because the passage contains no mention of sacrifices
Because He required only money
medium.explanation: The Lord distinguishes the neglected offerings from the sins that burdened Him.
medium.q: Why is the Lord not complaining that sacrifices themselves are wrong?

answers: A costly offering or incense ingredient
A road through the wilderness
A weapon of war
medium.explanation: Sweet cane is mentioned with money, incense, and sacrificial offerings.
medium.q: What is “sweet cane” in this passage?

answers: Israel failed to maintain a true relationship of dependence and worship toward the Lord
Israel called upon the Lord constantly
Israel did not know Jacob’s name
challenge.explanation: The complaint concerns Israel’s failure to turn genuinely to the Lord in worship and dependence.
challenge.q: What does “thou hast not called upon me” mean beyond merely failing to speak?

answers: It moves from failure to call upon the Lord, to neglected offerings, to accumulated sins
It moves from praise, to gathering, to redemption
It moves from war, to water, to creation
challenge.explanation: The passage begins with Israel’s failure to call, describes neglected worship, and ends with its sins and iniquities.
challenge.q: How does the argument develop through these verses?

answers: The heavy burden of Israel’s sins upon the Lord
The joy caused by Israel’s worship
The perfection of Israel’s sacrifices
challenge.explanation: These expressions stress how seriously the Lord regards Israel’s sins.
challenge.q: What does the repetition of “made me to serve” and “wearied me” emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Erasing Sin and Judging Israel’s Leaders

answers: The Lord alone
The nations
Israel’s leaders
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions.”

answers: Plead together in judgment
Go to war
Trade with the nations
easy.explanation: He says, “Put me in remembrance: let us plead together.”
easy.q: What does the Lord invite Israel to do?

answers: Israel’s first father and teachers
The beasts of the field
The Chaldeans alone
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Thy first father hath sinned, and thy teachers have transgressed against me.”
easy.q: Who is said to have sinned and transgressed?

answers: The Lord can blot out sin while still calling Israel to account
Judgment always makes forgiveness impossible
The two ideas are unrelated
medium.explanation: The Lord promises to blot out transgressions but also summons Israel to plead and be justified.
medium.q: How are forgiveness and judgment related in this passage?

answers: The profaning of the sanctuary’s princes and reproach upon Israel
The gathering of Israel
Protection from the fire
medium.explanation: The Lord says He profaned the princes of the sanctuary and gave Jacob to the curse and Israel to reproaches.
medium.q: What results from the sins of Israel’s fathers and leaders?

answers: That Israel may present its case and be examined
That Israel may escape the discussion
That Israel may rule the nations
medium.explanation: The Lord invites Israel to declare its case in the legal setting of the passage.
medium.q: What does “that thou mayest be justified” mean in this setting?

answers: The Lord offers forgiveness while holding Israel responsible for its sins
The passage contrasts only water and fire
The passage concerns gathering without any mention of sin
challenge.explanation: The Lord blots out transgressions, yet the passage also stresses judgment and responsibility.
challenge.q: What tension is present in these verses?

answers: It emphasizes that forgiveness comes from the Lord’s own will and action
It says Israel erased its own sins
It denies that sin existed
challenge.explanation: The phrase identifies the Lord Himself as the source and reason for the act of forgiveness.
challenge.q: Why does the Lord say He blots out transgressions “for mine own sake”?

answers: It reminds the reader that redemption stands alongside sin, judgment, and consequences
It completely cancels every promise of redemption
It changes to an unrelated subject
challenge.explanation: The ending balances the Lord’s mercy with a serious account of Israel’s sin and its consequences.
challenge.q: How does the ending alter the tone of the chapter’s earlier promises?
